summary: Careful Resume is a cautious method for fast startup of congestion control. It reuses parameters computed from previously observed path characteristics between the same two endpoints, saved from an earlier connection, to adjust the behavior of a later one. This is a Standards Track document.

eli5.summary: If you remember a road was clear yesterday, you can start fast today, but you still watch carefully in case things changed.

questions: reuse path state for new connections
subtitle: How a new connection can safely reuse what an earlier one learned about the path, instead of starting slow again.

tldr.problem: A congestion control algorithm starts slowly and takes time to get up to speed, which wastes time on paths with a large bandwidth-delay product, even when an earlier connection already learned how much the path can carry.
tldr.mechanism: Careful Resume saves the capacity and minimum RTT seen on a path, checks that the path still looks the same, then paces a jump to at most half the saved window, validates it, and retreats to a safe value if congestion appears.
tldr.outcome: A sender can finish transfers sooner on high-delay paths while limiting harm to other flows. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: RTT path-change hint
facts.value: Current RTT more than 10 times saved_rtt

today: RFC 9959 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2026, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Startup Is Slow
sections.content:
Every Internet transport must either use a congestion control (CC) algorithm or limit its sending rate. A CC algorithm normally ramps up slowly in its Slow Start phase, so that it does not overshoot the capacity of the path. That caution costs time, especially on paths with a high Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP).

RFC 9959 specifies Careful Resume. It targets transfers where the congestion window (CWND) is the limit, meaning the transfer wants to send far more than the initial window (IW) allows and the path BDP is much larger than the IW times the RTT. It is based on temporal sharing (sometimes called caching) of CC parameters saved from an earlier connection between the same endpoints.

The RFC gives one example: over a geo-stationary satellite access network, a 5.3 MB transfer could take 9 seconds with standard CC but 4 seconds with Careful Resume. The method does not cover broadcast or multicast destinations.
sections.eli5: When you start a long walk you begin slowly to be safe. If you already know the path is wide open, you can speed up sooner, as long as you stay careful.

sections.title: Three Safety Precautions
sections.content:
Reusing old numbers trades faster transfers against the risk of harming other connections that share the same bottleneck. The RFC builds in three precautions.

  • Reconnaissance Phase: first check that the saved values still fit. The sender sends no more than a normal new connection would, then proceeds only if the path looks the same and no congestion is seen.
  • Unvalidated Phase: jump the window to no more than a fraction (one half) of the saved value, and pace every unvalidated packet, so flows that arrived since the last measurement are not starved.
  • Safe Retreat Phase: if congestion shows up, drop the window to no more than what a standard process would have found, so that trying and failing does not unduly hurt existing connections.

Rate-based algorithms follow the same principle. A sender using BBR, for example, sets its pacing rate to half the remembered bottleneck bandwidth.
sections.eli5: It is like trying a shortcut: check it still looks the same, step onto it gently, and back off at once if it turns out to be crowded.

sections.title: Saved Parameters and the Remote Endpoint
sections.content:
While a connection is established, it can save a set of CC parameters for the path to its Remote Endpoint. This is an implementation-dependent value that identifies the sender's view of the path: an identifier for the sending interface and an identifier for the destination, and optionally the DSCP. Adding more information separates paths better but makes saved values reusable less often.

The saved set contains:

  • saved_cwnd: the capacity used, measured as the bytes sent during one RTT. If this is less than four times the IW, the sender can choose not to save it.
  • saved_rtt: the minimum RTT at the time of observation.
  • a Lifetime, after which the set must not be used.

A sender MUST NOT keep more than one set for a Remote Endpoint, and SHOULD update or replace it after a later observation. The RFC warns against saving a CWND overshoot from the end of Slow Start, and suggests discounting observations made while the sender was rate limited.

The Lifetime is configurable. A small value (minutes) suits dynamic paths or bottlenecks shared by many senders. A longer one (hours) can suit stable paths. RFC 7661 suggests an unvalidated period of no more than five minutes, but the RFC argues a longer period can be justified here because of the extra safeguards.
sections.eli5: Careful Resume writes a note after each trip: how much traffic fit and how long it took. The note has an expiry date, and you only keep one note per route.

sections.title: The Phases of Careful Resume
sections.content:
In the Reconnaissance Phase the CWND starts at the IW and normal CC keeps running. The sender stops using Careful Resume if it detects congestion (for example packet loss or ECN-CE marking), if another connection has already used the saved_cwnd, if the Remote Endpoint changed, if the Lifetime expired, or if the minimum RTT is less than or equal to saved_rtt / 2. Once all the initial data is acknowledged without congestion, it MAY enter the Unvalidated Phase.

In the Unvalidated Phase the variable PipeSize starts at the flight size and the CWND is set to jump_cwnd, which MUST be no more than half of saved_cwnd and no more than max_jump. All packets MUST be paced using the current RTT. Congestion or a detected path change sends the sender to the Safe Retreat Phase. Sending all unvalidated packets, an ACK for the first unvalidated packet, or more than one RTT elapsing moves it to the Validating Phase, unless the sender was rate limited, in which case the CWND is reset to PipeSize and normal CC resumes.

The Validating Phase usually lasts about one RTT. The CWND grows by normal rules while PipeSize tracks acknowledged data. Congestion leads to Safe Retreat. An ACK for the last unvalidated packet means the jump was safe, and Careful Resume ends.

In the Safe Retreat Phase the saved parameters are deleted and the CWND MUST be reduced to no more than PipeSize / 2. It MUST NOT grow while in this phase. When the last unvalidated packet is acknowledged, the sender leaves, and ssthresh MUST be set to no more than PipeSize * Beta. Beta is between 0.5 and 1, with a default of 0.5. Persistent congestion, such as an RTO, also ends Careful Resume.
sections.eli5: There are four steps: look around, step forward gently, check nothing bad happened, and if it did, back up a lot further than you stepped.

sections.title: Path Checks, Pacing and Transport Limits
sections.content:
To confirm the path, the sender compares saved_rtt with each current RTT sample. A sample less than half of saved_rtt signals a path change, because the jump is half of the saved window and the rate should not exceed what was observed. A current RTT more than ten times saved_rtt is also taken as a path change. A larger RTT only lowers the pacing rate, so it stays safe.

Pacing uses the current RTT rather than the saved one, which avoids a small saved_rtt inflating the rate. The RFC gives an example pacing interval, where MPS is the maximum packet size including headers.

Only one connection at a time may use a given saved_cwnd. This prevents several concurrent connections from each jumping based on the same saved value. Servers behind load balancers may need a distributed method to enforce this.

Other limits can hide the benefit. A TCP sender is bounded by the receiver window, and a QUIC receiver might need to issue proactive MAX_DATA frames to raise flow control limits. Receivers may also ask to enable or inhibit Careful Resume, for example when they know a path or local interface has changed.
sections.eli5: You compare the clock times from the last trip with this one. If they are very different, you assume the route changed and do not trust the old note.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Careful Resume is a sender-side change designed to limit harm to other flows. Its use can be constrained in three ways: the configured maximum jump (max_jump), the Remote Endpoint that decides which client and server may use a set of saved parameters, and the configured Lifetime.

Equal Cost Multipath Routing, Anycast Routing and Network Address Translation can change the forwarding path. Their effect is smaller if the alternative paths are provisioned with equivalent capacity. With anycast, a client cannot tell which server or server farm it will reach. If all servers behind an address are in one location, they could coordinate sharing of saved parameters. If a later connection might take a very different path that cannot support the same capacity, a sender should not use Careful Resume.
sections.eli5: If several roads lead to the same place and some are narrow, an old note about the wide one may be wrong, so grown-ups should plan for that.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security considerations are the same as for other sender-based congestion control methods. These rely on the receiver acknowledging data honestly, and how far an on-path or off-path attacker can influence CC depends on the security properties of the transport protocol in use.

The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The sender trusts the receiver to say honestly what arrived, just as with any other way of controlling speed.
